CA-2025-AB1539.s: This law requires each qualified political party, and certain independent or write-in presidential candidates, to certify to the Secretary of State that their presidential and vice presidential nominees are qualified to be elected President under the Twenty-Second Amendment. If the required certification is not made on time, the candidates’ names cannot be placed on the ballot or certified list. It applies to political parties, independent presidential candidates, write-in presidential candidates, and groups of presidential electors.

CA-2025-AB1581.s: This law requires the State Department of Education to post statewide data on pupils who identify as American Indian or Alaska Native on its website. The data must cover the prior school year and include the number of pupils, academic achievement, suspension and expulsion rates, chronic absenteeism, and four- and five-year graduation rates. It applies to pupils who identify as American Indian or Alaska Native only, as well as pupils who identify as American Indian or Alaska Native along with another race or ethnicity.

CA-2025-AB1608.s: This bill would rename the Office of the Inspector General, High-Speed Rail, and change the title of the Inspector General. It would let the Inspector General use pay and job classifications from other state agencies doing similar oversight work, and contract for needed goods and services. For contracts up to $1,000,000, it would exempt the office from certain Public Contract Code and state information technology review requirements.

CA-2025-AB1645.s: This law changes prison visitation rules for incarcerated people and their visitors. It says the rules must recognize the importance of nonsexual physical contact during visits and must not unreasonably restrict it. It also says staff must give a clear warning and a chance to correct minor contact issues before ending a visit or taking discipline. The law still lets the department search, supervise visits, and use limits needed to stop contraband.

CA-2025-AB1665.s: This law adds mental health training to the California High School Coaching Education and Training Program. Starting with the 2027–28 school year, high school coaches in California Interscholastic Federation programs must complete initial training and then training every two years on mental health before the season starts. School districts, county offices of education, and charter schools that offer other athletic programs must also make sure their coaches complete training every two years on sudden cardiac arrest and youth athletics behavioral and mental health training.

CA-2025-AB1679.s: This law requires cities, counties, and city and county governments to allow a temporary commercial activation authorization for a pop-up small business in an eligible commercial space for up to 120 days. Local governments may temporarily suspend, defer, or modify some standards tied to permanent occupancy, but the temporary use still must meet health, safety, and accessibility rules. The law also requires written accessibility guidance for applicants and lets local governments set fees, enforcement rules, and penalties within program costs. It also adds approved pop-up small businesses doing limited food preparation to the definition of “food facility.”

CA-2025-AB1697.s: This law changes when certain employment contract limits take effect. It applies the ban on stay-or-pay terms to contracts entered into on or after January 1, 2027, instead of January 1, 2026. It also adds exceptions for some government-backed repayment programs, certain tuition repayment contracts, apprenticeship contracts, some bonus repayment agreements, and some advanced paid time off repayment obligations. Workers covered by these rules can bring a civil action for violations.

CA-2025-AB1713.s: This law requires California public colleges and universities to accept certain disability documents as verification when a student asks for academic accommodations. It bars them from making a student get a new or extra diagnostic evaluation just to prove a disability shown in those documents. The schools may still ask for other information needed to decide what accommodations are appropriate, but they do not have to provide the exact services listed in the student’s plan.

CA-2025-AB1740.s: This law requires the City of Santa Monica to submit a complete local coastal program for its part of the coastal zone by January 1, 2029. It gives the Coastal Commission deadlines to review the city’s proposal, share any issues in writing, and send quarterly updates to the Legislature if it does not act in time. It also changes how some coastal permit and local coastal program amendments are handled for projects that convert road right-of-way into bicycle, transit, or pedestrian space, and it requires yearly reports on those applications through 2032.

CA-2025-AB1763.s: This law makes a pupil’s absence for a holiday or ceremony of the pupil’s religion a required excused absence. It removes the need for the parent or guardian to request the absence in writing and for the principal or a designated representative to approve it. It affects pupils, parents or guardians, and local educational agencies and schools.

CA-2025-AB1816.s: This law lets a court extend probation for up to one more year for a person who must register as a sex offender, if the probation department asks for it and the court finds the person has not completed probation and needs more time for programming. The court may make this decision based on the person’s progress in treatment, compliance with supervision, and public safety and rehabilitation. It also says local agencies and school districts must be reimbursed for state-mandated costs if the state board decides the act creates those costs.

CA-2025-AB1876.s: This law bars health care service plans and health insurers from excluding people from enrollment, denying benefits, or discriminating against them based on race, color, national origin, age, disability, or sex. It says sex discrimination includes intersex traits, pregnancy or related conditions, sexual orientation, gender identity, and sex stereotypes. It also limits plans and insurers from denying or restricting coverage for services tied to sex assigned at birth, gender identity, or gender otherwise recorded, including services related to gender transition or other "gender-affirming care" in the text. They must also give enrollees and insureds notice about how to file a discrimination grievance.

CA-2025-AB1918.s: This law adds body art facilities to the list of places that must post a human trafficking notice. It also requires these facilities to give at least 20 minutes of human trafficking training to employees and registered practitioners who may come into contact with a victim or receive a report of suspected human trafficking. The training must cover how to recognize and report human trafficking, and it may include evidence-based, trauma-informed material from nonprofit groups and information from the Department of Justice website.

CA-2025-AB1940.s: This bill would change state civil rights law to include perimenopause, menopause, postmenopause, and related medical conditions in the definitions of “sex” and “medical condition” under FEHA and the Unruh Civil Rights Act. It would also require the Civil Rights Department to update its employment discrimination poster to notify people about rights and protections related to those conditions. The changes would affect employers, business establishments, and people covered by these laws.

CA-2025-AB1941.s: This law creates the crime of organized metal theft. It covers people who work together to steal, receive, buy, or possess metal materials knowing or believing they were stolen, or who plan, organize, or finance the theft. A violation can be punished as either a misdemeanor or a felony. It affects people involved in stealing or handling stolen metal materials and can also apply to scrap metal transactions tied to those crimes.

CA-2025-AB1985.s: This law requires certain college and university campuses to make coaches and trainers in athletic programs complete student mental health training as a condition of working or volunteering. The training must include suicide prevention education and be done by July 1, 2028, and every 2 years after that. It applies to California State University campuses, community colleges, and private postsecondary and independent institutions that receive state financial assistance, and it requests the same from University of California campuses.

CA-2025-AB1987.s: This law changes how the Department of Fish and Wildlife handles permits, leases, and hunting program funds on department-managed lands. It requires the department to use the Automated License Data System to sell entry permits for consumptive use, adds wetland floodup to the topics hunters can comment on, and creates a new fund for waterfowl hunting reservation and entry pass revenues from Type A and Type B Wildlife Areas. It also says agricultural lease money and other listed funds must be used, when appropriated by the Legislature, for managing, maintaining, restoring, and operating department-managed lands.

CA-2025-AB1997.s: The bill would change the review process for some housing development projects under California’s environmental review and permit rules. It would require a public agency to approve or deny a housing development project within 30 days after the lead agency certifies the environmental report, if certain conditions are met. It was vetoed by the Governor.

CA-2025-AB2038.s: This law requires insurers to keep renewing certain residential property insurance policies for at least three annual renewal periods, or at least 36 months after a total loss caused by a disaster, if the loss was not due to the insured’s negligence and the property has not become uninsurable for later reasons. It also bars insurers from canceling or refusing to renew residential property insurance for properties in ZIP Codes within or next to a fire perimeter for two years after a state of emergency is declared, based only on the wildfire location. These rules affect homeowners with residential property insurance and insurers that write those policies.

CA-2025-AB2076.s: This law adds nitrous oxide to the list of products that sellers in California must keep from being sold to minors. It also bars online sellers from letting buyers use gift cards or store credit for certain products that are illegal to sell to minors. Public prosecutors may seek civil penalties, injunctive relief, and attorney’s fees and costs for violations.

CA-2025-AB2128.s: This law bars housing authorities and other covered housing providers from using term limits or work requirements as a condition for getting or keeping covered housing, unless federal law requires it. It also bars rules that change the amount of rent subsidy or assistance based on those limits or requirements. Covered housing providers may still offer voluntary employment or job training programs if participation does not affect eligibility or assistance. The law does not change certain federal housing programs and requirements.

CA-2025-AB2146.s: This law requires the California Interagency Council on Homelessness to complete a statewide study of the coordinated entry system and its role in connecting people and families experiencing homelessness to affordable housing. The study must look at how the system works, how effective it is, what delays or barriers exist, and where state, local, and federal requirements affect housing placement. The council must consult a broad group of stakeholders and post the report on its website and send it to the Legislature and relevant policy committees.

CA-2025-AB2218.s: This bill would require state government agencies to support California Native American tribes in maintaining cultural and linguistic traditions, practicing ecosystem stewardship, and consulting in good faith on policies that may affect tribal communities. It would set state water policy to recognize and address water inequities affecting California Native American tribes through financial assistance, protection of tribal beneficial uses, consultation on water projects and policies, and use of indigenous knowledge. It would also require certain state agencies to use that policy when making water-related rules, permits, or grant criteria, and to offer financial assistance to tribes when allowed by law. The bill would require mediation through the Governor’s Office of Tribal Affairs before certain disputes between tribes and state agencies could be challenged in court.

CA-2025-AB2257.s: This law lets a county board of supervisors create a jail administrator position by resolution. The sheriff must nominate a candidate, and the board must confirm or deny that person after a public hearing. A jail administrator would have supervisory authority over county jails and incarcerated people, while the sheriff would keep some authority to supervise, direct, evaluate, discipline, or remove the jail administrator. In counties with a jail administrator, the usual rule that the sheriff alone keeps the county jail would not apply, and "sheriff" would include the jail administrator for jail-related duties.

CA-2025-AB2297.s: This law requires courts to order restitution to victims when a defendant enters a diversion program, if the defendant is given a chance for a hearing or waives it. If the court finds restitution is owed, payment must be ordered during diversion. A defendant’s inability to pay because of indigence or mental disorder cannot be used to deny diversion or to find the defendant failed to comply with diversion terms.

CA-2025-AB2367.s: This bill would require certain state departments to report quarterly information about their state-run health facilities. The reports would cover vacancies, overtime, registry contract data, and times when a facility did not meet required staffing minimums, along with an explanation. The information would go to the relevant employee representatives and be posted on a public website.

CA-2025-AB2405.s: This law requires a peace officer who is transporting a person for mental health assessment to take the person to the closest appropriate designated facility, based on distance or travel time. If an emergency department is the most appropriate place, the officer must take the person to the closest appropriate emergency department. The person may tell the officer which facility they prefer, as long as that does not unreasonably delay care or greatly change the route. The law does not apply to the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation or California Correctional Health Care Services.

CA-2025-AB2463.s: This law requires the Public Utilities Commission to include more detailed information in decisions about the authorized return on equity for electrical corporations and gas corporations in cost of capital proceedings. It must describe the financial models, inputs, weights, calculations, and any changes from prior methodology, and explain the link between credit quality and the authorized return on equity. The commission must also give the Legislature an annual analysis of trends in California corporation credit ratings as part of its annual report.

CA-2025-AB2465.s: This bill would make certain business entities ineligible for state grants, loans, and some tax credits if they are directly invested in, own, operate, or manage a private detention facility, or if they contract with the federal government for immigration enforcement purposes. It would also make some taxpayers ineligible for certain tax credits if they meet the bill’s definition of a disqualified taxpayer. The bill would create the Due Process for All Fund and direct money into it for immigration-related services and programs.

CA-2025-AB2524.s: This law lets a county probation department or county child welfare agency issue work permits to minors who are under the jurisdiction of a juvenile court. It applies to minors who are wards of the court or dependent children of the court, and the permit must be in the minor’s best interest and be treated as valid like a school-issued permit. School districts, charter schools, and private schools may still issue work permits and may revoke permits issued by a county probation department or county child welfare agency.

CA-2025-AB2534.s: This law adds forced marriage to California’s Domestic Violence Prevention Act. It defines forced marriage as a marriage entered or kept through force, fraud, coercion, duress, abuse of power, or coercive control, even if the marriage is not legally valid. Courts may treat conduct to arrange, officiate, finance, or help a forced marriage as domestic violence and may issue orders to stop it. The law also lets courts order the surrender of passports, visas, or other travel or identity documents in cases involving forced marriage or a credible risk of it.

CA-2025-AB2599.s: This law requires certain businesses in California with annual worldwide gross receipts over $100 million to file an affidavit about records tied to slavery, including whether they bought or sold enslaved persons, used them as collateral, or helped finance those transactions. It also requires the Civil Rights Department to create a public digital platform with the affidavits, records, and related reports if the Legislature makes an appropriation. Businesses that bid on or renew certain state contracts must also certify that they have filed the affidavit and that they comply with the Unruh Civil Rights Act and the California Fair Employment and Housing Act.

CA-2025-AB2647.s: The law requires the Energy Commission to prepare a comprehensive assessment of advanced nuclear technologies and the potential for new nuclear powerplants in California. The assessment must look at costs, reliability, waste management, public health, siting, workforce needs, and possible changes to state law and regulations. The commission must consult with other state agencies and hold workshops for a wide range of stakeholders, and public agencies may evaluate nuclear energy for long-term resource needs.

CA-2025-AB2684.s: This law lets county social workers or probation officers offer nonminor dependents who are placed out of state a virtual option for their monthly visit. The nonminor dependent must give informed consent, and the virtual visit must include a private discussion and video for both sides; the visit can be changed to in-person if requested or if there are safety or well-being concerns. It also requires at least one in-person visit each quarter and directs the state department to convene a working group to develop guidelines for county placing agencies and attorneys representing these nonminor dependents.

CA-2025-AB2706.s: This law adds rules for commercial manufacturing, processing, or packing of acidified foods and low-acid foods for people or animals. It requires a person to be registered with the department and to have a scheduled process from a processing authority before doing that work. It also says foods made without that scheduled process are misbranded. People who make, pack, or hold these foods and need a scheduled process must pay an extra annual $350 fee for food safety inspections and reviews.

CA-2025-AB2713.s: This law changes rules for large online platforms about content provenance data and digital signatures. It requires platforms to detect this data, show users information about whether content was generated or altered by a generative AI system or captured by a device, and let users inspect system provenance data in an accessible way. It also says platforms do not have to keep, show, or let users download personal information, and do not have to act on provenance data or digital signatures that do not follow widely adopted standards.

CA-2025-AB706.s: This law creates the FOREST program and the FOREST and Wildfire Prevention Fund to support biomass power generation and revitalize idle biomass facilities. It lets money from the Timber Fund or the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund be used for reimbursements to certain facilities that use forest biomass waste to make electricity and meet other requirements. It also changes how the Timber Fund can be spent and gives the new fund and program a place in those funding priorities.

CA-2025-AB801.s: This law requires the financial regulator to examine certain banks, credit unions, and residential mortgage lenders or servicers for compliance with nondiscrimination laws tied to mortgage lending. It also makes a violation of those laws a violation of the Financial Code and allows enforcement action. The law requires written findings to be shared with the regulated entity’s leaders and limits disclosure of those findings.

CA-2025-SB1000.s: California law would change rules for AI content labels and disclosure tools. It would require a provider of a covered AI system to offer a disclosure verification tool, remove the user-size cutoff for covered providers, and change what must be shown in the hidden label for AI-made or AI-changed images, video, or audio. It would also delay part of the rules for AI systems mainly meant as assistive technology and bar a provider from wrongly saying a system is such a tool.

CA-2025-SB1009.s: This law limits when a court can place a minor in juvenile hall or other locked care. The court must find that a less strict option will not work before ordering detention or other physical confinement, and it can look again at detention if new information comes up. Before a child is taken from a parent or guardian, the court must consider whether reasonable steps were made to avoid removal and whether services could help the child return home.

CA-2025-SB1012.s: This law helps people who finish the California Conservation Camp program move into state-approved apprenticeship programs for construction craft laborer jobs after release. It says that, starting July 1, 2027, successful time in the program counts as qualifying experience for that apprenticeship. The department and the state fire agency must also give eligible people a written certificate to show they can apply.

CA-2025-SB1030.s: Passed in 2026, this law ends a rule that required an unrelated adult man living with a family to pay money to the family when the family applies for or gets CalWORKs aid. The change starts July 1, 2027, or later if set that way. It affects families in the CalWORKs cash aid program and the local agencies that run it.

CA-2025-SB1051.s: This law changes how child care navigators help foster children get into the Emergency Child Care Bridge Program. It lets them send a foster child to the county welfare department for review, and the county must decide if the child can get the program. It affects foster children and the county offices that run the program.

CA-2025-SB1085.s: This law changes when cities and counties must ask water systems to check whether a housing project has enough water planned for it. It requires them to make that check earlier for certain housing projects and requires the water system to send the water supply report within 45 days, instead of 90 days, without a public meeting to approve it. A city or county may also go to court to force a water system to provide the report.

CA-2025-SB1087.s: The bill changes how California regions make long-term travel plans tied to lower greenhouse gas emissions. It would move the main sustainable communities strategy to an 8-year cycle with a 4-year progress report, and it would have the state air board give regions reduction targets for 2035 and 2045 after holding technical workshops. It also changes how the state reviews those plans, repeals some current reporting rules for San Diego and Sacramento, and updates the state transportation plan to use performance measures in project planning.

CA-2025-SB1090.s: This law changes some housing and subdivision rules for projects in ZIP codes 91001 and 91003, which cover Altadena, for applications filed on or after October 1, 2026. For those projects, the usual fast-track local approval rules would not apply until January 1, 2030, with some exceptions. It took effect right away as an urgency law.

CA-2025-SB1094.s: This law changes how pharmacists can swap one biologic drug for another, including biosimilar drugs, when a prescriber has not said not to substitute. It also limits health plans and health insurers from stopping coverage for a drug that was already approved, if the patient still needs it and it is safe and effective, and it lets them require a tried biosimilar or similar biologic in some cases. For plans and policies issued, changed, or renewed on or after January 1, 2027, if a drug list includes a reference product, it must also include at least one lower-cost biosimilar or interchangeable biologic for that same product.

CA-2025-SB1099.s: The law clarifies that cities, counties, city and county governments, and hospital districts may give aid, including health care, as a state or local public benefit. It affects people who meet a local program's rules, including some people without lawful status in the U.S. The bill became law on September 30, 2026.

CA-2025-SB1105.s: The bill would change when some federal law officers and certain federal workers can make arrests or have peace officer status in California. It would also let deputized tribal officers of the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs make arrests tied to their federal duties, and it would set new rules for local law enforcement interagency agreements, including a written ban on racial or identity profiling. Some existing agreements would stay valid until July 1, 2027, and then need to be updated. The bill was vetoed by the Governor.

CA-2025-SB1167.s: This law changes which vehicles can be sold or labeled as electric bicycles and adds new rules for mopeds and motor-driven cycles. It updates the definitions of those vehicles, changes the buyer disclosure rules, and adds label details for electric bicycles and certification labels for mopeds and motor-driven cycles. It also applies to sellers, manufacturers, and importers, and it became law on September 30, 2026.

CA-2025-SB1192.s: This bill, which became law in 2026, sets up a court process for a domestic violence victim to ask for a prefiling order in a case already in court. If the court finds the other party is the abuser and the filing or discovery was frivolous or abusive, that person would need court permission before filing more papers or asking for discovery against the victim. The bill also lets people seek to end the order, adds possible sanctions, attorney fees, and costs for violations, and waives filing fees for related filings. It also allows free electronic filing and remote appearances in these hearings, and requires courts to send these orders to the Judicial Council.

CA-2025-SB1203.s: The bill became law and changes training rules for certain proprietary private security workers starting January 1, 2029. It would require 42 hours of training, including a course on arrest powers and proper use of force, plus yearly training that includes 4 hours on deescalation and 2 hours on workers' rights. It would also require employers to pay workers for training, raise some fines, and expand when workplace altercation reports must be filed.

CA-2025-SB1209.s: The law changes how the Insurance Commissioner can handle insurer exams. If an exam report finds problems, the insurer must fix them and may face a penalty if it does not. If the commissioner thinks the insurer did not follow the report, the commissioner can hold a hearing and order the insurer to pay a penalty and carry out the report's fixes.

CA-2025-SB1246.s: This law changes rules for self-driving vehicles on California roads. It requires makers of these vehicles to keep enough remote support capacity, use remote drivers in the United States with the right California license, and send local help quickly after a crash or other incident. It also gives emergency workers more authority to move or stop certain driverless commercial vehicles and sets a 2028 deadline for state guidelines on response times.

CA-2025-SB1255.s: This law creates a state label for colleges and universities that do a strong job serving Latino students, if money is set aside for it. It sets up a board to give out the label and names the California State University chancellor’s office to handle the application process. A school’s label would last 5 years.

CA-2025-SB1296.s: California law now requires landlords or their agents to put their pet policy in writing and share it on the property website, in digital ads, and in rental search listings. They must also give a written copy with any rental application, and the policy must spell out the rules and duties for tenants with pets. If an application fee is charged without first sharing the pet policy, and the renter then cannot or will not move forward because of that, the fee must be refunded if requested. These rules take effect April 1, 2027.

CA-2025-SB1359.s: The law requires gas companies to give the California Public Utilities Commission a yearly report on what they spend on gas pipe replacement and upgrade projects. It also asks the commission to consider a plan for how those gas pipes lose value over time, so future gas customers may face less risk from paying for old assets that are no longer needed. The measure affects gas corporations and the state utility commission, and it became law on September 30, 2026.

CA-2025-SB1365.s: This bill became law and changes California’s price gouging rules during a state or local emergency. It would make some rent increases for housing during an emergency an offense, and it would change some current exceptions into defenses a person can use in court. It would also expand the housing covered by these rules and change how rent is figured for some places rented by the day.

CA-2025-SB1383.s: California law on housing density bonuses was changed to limit some local incentives for taller buildings. For buildings over 85 feet, local governments may not count certain site, zoning, design, or other labor-related changes as density bonus incentives or concessions if they include labor standards adopted by the local government. The labor standards tied to this rule are those that do not go beyond certain state requirements as they stood on December 31, 2025.

CA-2025-SB1387.s: This law requires state agencies that collect demographic data to use a separate category for Jewish ancestry or ethnicity, and to include that data in reports released on or after January 1, 2030. It also says state agencies must protect privacy, keep personal identifying information confidential, and limit how they use the data. The Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation must also let people self-identify as Jewish in its race or ethnic origin data.

CA-2025-SB1388.s: Creates a new state program in the Department of Housing and Community Development to help affordable housing providers reduce risk and find better insurance options. The department would develop tools and help, and it could also use outside experts to give one-on-one support or make those tools available more widely. It was approved by the Governor and chaptered into law in 2026.

CA-2025-SB1401.s: This law changes court rules for people found not mentally competent to stand trial. It lets a county behavioral health agency share certain private medical information with the court to help decide if a person can get behavioral health services, and it changes when charges must be dismissed in some cases. It also says a person may be found "gravely disabled" under either of two listed standards, and it lets a court send some misdemeanor cases for county conservatorship if the court itself thinks the person appears gravely disabled.

CA-2025-SB1406.s: This law changes how California decides when a vehicle, boat, or plane bought through a company is treated as being for use in the state and may owe use tax. It adds rules for partnerships and shell companies, which are paper companies used to hide who really owns them, and can make certain officers, managers, partners, owners, or members personally liable for unpaid tax, interest, and penalties. It took effect right away as a tax law.

CA-2025-SB1414.s: The bill would create a 14-member citizens redistricting commission for San Bernardino County, if the Legislature provides funding. The commission would draw the county Board of Supervisors district lines and follow set rules and deadlines. It became law in 2026.

CA-2025-SB1423.s: The bill became law and requires the state planning office to collect, standardize, keep up to date, and post online a core set of statewide planning data by July 1, 2028. The data would include things like hazard areas, natural resource sensitivity, and farm value data. It also directs the office to give agencies guidance by January 1, 2029 on using this data in regional planning, and local, regional, and state governments may use it for land use and infrastructure plans.

CA-2025-SB331.s: This law requires large group health plans and health insurance policies to cover hearing aids and related services for people under 21, if they are medically needed. The coverage applies to plans and policies issued, changed, or renewed on or after January 1, 2028. A plan may cap coverage at $3,000 for each hearing aid device.

CA-2025-SB342.s: This law changes when a contractor or a person using an unlicensed contractor can sue over payment on certain projects. For public works, commercial construction projects, institutional construction projects, common interest developments without a tenant or resident party to the contract, and multifamily residential projects with four or more units without a tenant or resident party, a contractor may seek payment if licensed when the contract was made and during the work claimed, and a customer may recover only the part paid for work done while the contractor was unlicensed. The law also keeps the general rule that unlicensed contractors cannot recover payment for work that requires a contractor’s license, except as provided in these cases.

CA-2025-SB401.s: California law now lets the Fair Political Practices Commission give some people up to 60 extra days to file reports under the Political Reform Act when an emergency makes it hard to file on time. This can apply to people in the affected area, but not during the 90 days before an election. The law covers candidates, committees, lobbyists, slate mailer groups, and public officials who must file these reports.

CA-2025-SB503.s: This law adds rules for artificial intelligence systems used to help make clinical decisions about timing of care, diagnosis, or treatment in health care settings. Developers and deployers must make reasonable efforts to identify systems with a known or reasonably foreseeable risk of biased impacts, and developers must share documentation about the system’s intended uses, risks, testing, and monitoring. Deployers must regularly monitor these systems and take reasonable steps to reduce biased impacts.

CA-2025-SB549.s: Heritage schools could serve younger children, including those under 4 years and 9 months old, if they are enrolled in kindergarten, including transitional kindergarten, or grades 1 to 12. When a child enrolls, the school would also have to tell parents or guardians that the state education department does not regulate heritage schools or monitor their classes. The bill became law in 2026.

CA-2025-SB626.s: This law changes rules for screening and treating mental health issues during pregnancy and after birth. It lets health care workers refer patients to another licensed worker for screening, and requires follow-up evaluation and treatment when a patient screens positive, if that is within the provider’s scope of practice. It also updates health plan and insurer programs to include pregnancy and postpartum screenings, case management or care help for people who screen positive, and guidance to providers.

CA-2025-SB661.s: Would move a set share of sales tax money from jet fuel into an airport fund each year and split it among airports and aviation programs. It would also require airports that sell or use jet fuel to report fuel flow data so the state can set each airport’s share. The bill was vetoed by the Governor.

CA-2025-SB677.s: The law changes how some joint powers agencies can work on housing finance and bond approvals. It says the state can join one of these agencies in limited cases to help approve bonds for certain rental housing projects, and it treats the state as part of the agency for that purpose only. It also changes some rules tied to subdivision map appeals and says the state joining an existing agency is not, by itself, a change in that agency's makeup.

CA-2025-SB685.s: This law changes rules for some private schools and agencies that provide special education services to students placed by local school districts. It removes the rule that these schools or agencies must be nonsectarian, but bars public money from paying for religious instruction and bars those schools or agencies from giving that instruction to placed students. It also requires certification that the services are secular, neutral, and respectful about religion, and it adds a ban on discrimination in providing these services.

CA-2025-SB690.s: This law changes who can sue over the use of a pen register or trap-and-trace device on a website, online app, or mobile app without a court order. In those cases, only the Attorney General may bring the action, instead of a person who was harmed. It also applies this rule to some pending claims filed within 2 years before the law took effect.

CA-2025-SB715.s: The bill would move some election deadlines earlier, including the date the Secretary of State must tell candidates who else is running for the same office. It would also require candidates to say under penalty of perjury that the ballot designation worksheet is true and correct. These changes affect election officials and candidates for partisan and voter-nominated offices, and the bill became law.

CA-2025-SB758.s: California law would bar retailers from selling nitrous oxide at any retail location, with some exceptions. Cities and counties could set stricter local rules, as long as they do not block legitimate uses. The bill also became law in 2026.

CA-2025-SB799.s: Passed into law, this measure changes how the South Bay Regional Housing Trust can use its money. It would let the trust fund the preservation of housing, and also plan, build, and preserve housing for moderate-income people and families using private money and certain public money. It would also change how the trust sets its board size, picks members and alternates, and chooses its chair and vice chair.

CA-2025-SB804.s: This law sets up safety rules for pipelines that carry hydrogen in California, and the State Fire Marshal would oversee the program. It would let the state charge yearly fees to pipeline operators, keep those fee and penalty money in state accounts for pipeline safety work, and rename the state pipeline safety fund. It also sets penalties for breaking the rules or damaging hydrogen pipeline signs, and it asks the Public Utilities Commission to report on the right rules for some pipelines that carry hydrogen blends.

CA-2025-SB837.s: Signed into law, this bill would require local Aging and Disability Resource Connection programs to give disaster and emergency preparedness education. The education would be aimed at older adults and people with disabilities, and would help them prepare for and stay safe during and after natural disasters and other emergencies. These programs already help people find long-term services and supports.

CA-2025-SB868.s: The law changes rules for portable solar devices until January 1, 2030. It exempts them from state and utility interconnection rules, and it bars electric utilities from making users pay certain fees or take some required steps, though utilities may use a simple online form to get basic device and address info. Starting January 1, 2030, it also bans the sale of some plug-in portable solar devices that do not meet the bill's definition.

CA-2025-SB905.s: This law requires the California Public Utilities Commission to look at lowering the allowed profit rate for some power company capital costs. It also requires the commission to study other ways to finance electric grid, power plant, and power line investments that could lower costs for ratepayers, and to have large power companies share public data on how much more their power lines could be used. The commission must send a report to the Legislature by December 31, 2028.

CA-2025-SB913.s: This law requires the California Public Utilities Commission to set up ways for grouped small energy sources, like home solar and batteries, to count toward power supply needs by June 30, 2028. It also lets power companies, electric service providers, and community choice groups use these resources in their required power plans and purchases. The commission must set rules so customers with net energy metering or net billing do not get paid twice for the same power.

CA-2025-SB918.s: The bill would change rules for passthrough windows at retail food facilities. It would drop the self-closing device rule for some smaller openings, require an air curtain or a self-closing device for openings up to 432 square inches, and require both for larger openings. It would also require these openings to be used only for food delivery, not as a regular door for workers or customers.

CA-2025-SB925.s: This law requires the state energy commission to make a plan for fusion energy in California and send it to lawmakers by December 31, 2029. The plan must cover research, how to help fusion energy move into the market, rules for permits and licenses, and how fusion could help meet clean energy goals. It also expands a state review program so certain facilities that make key fusion energy parts can seek faster environmental approval.

CA-2025-SB930.s: California law now requires businesses that provide test proctoring services for classroom or course exams to use end-to-end encryption. That means the test data must be scrambled on the sender’s device and stay unreadable until it reaches the intended recipient, including the proctoring business. The rule applies to services for school districts, county education offices, and charter schools, starting July 1, 2027.

CA-2025-SB932.s: California law now requires an assignee, the person or group that got the claim, to name the original owner of the claim in the case title on the first paper they file in a court case. It applies to civil cases where someone is suing in the name of the real party in interest, which means the person or group with the right to bring the case. The bill was approved and chaptered in 2026.

CA-2025-SB938.s: The bill would change how some people can get a waiver from basic peace officer training in California. It would say that service as a sworn federal law enforcement officer, when that work was mainly immigration inspection, border enforcement, or arresting, detaining, or removing noncitizens, by itself does not count as enough training or experience for that waiver. It was vetoed by the Governor.

CA-2025-SB941.s: The law sets a price cap for items sold in commissaries, or small stores, at private detention facilities run by for-profit companies under contract with a government. The sale price of each item cannot be more than 35% above what the vendor charged for it. It affects private detention facilities and the people who buy items there.

CA-2025-SB951.s: California law now requires added notice when a mass layoff, move, or shutdown is caused in whole or in large part by AI or other automated tools. The notice must include details like which job tasks will be automated, and the labor agency must post summaries of these notices online and share quarterly statewide totals. The agency must also report to lawmakers by January 1, 2028, on how AI affects hiring and jobs across the state.

CA-2025-SB983.s: This law lets the San Diego Unified Port District try job order contracting for certain work under a pilot program. It sets limits of $5 million for one contract and $1 million for one job, and the first contract can last up to 12 months, with extensions as allowed. The district must report to the Legislature by January 1, 2035, and the program ends on January 1, 2037.
